"**Annabel Lee**" is the last complete poem[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-1) composed by American author Edgar Allan Poe. Like many of Poe's poems, it explores the theme of the death of a beautiful woman.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) The narrator, who fell in love with Annabel Lee when they were young, has a love for her so strong that even angels are envious. He retains his love for her after her death. There has been debate over who, if anyone, was the inspiration for "Annabel Lee". Though many women have been suggested, Poe's wife Virginia Eliza Clemm Poe is one of the more credible candidates. Written in 1849, it was not published until shortly after Poe's death that same year.
Poe's manuscript for "Annabel Lee", Columbia University Rare Book and Manuscript Library
The poem's narrator describes his love for Annabel Lee, which began many years ago in a "kingdom by the sea". Though they were young, their love for each other burned with such intensity that even angels were envious. For this reason, the narrator believes the seraphim caused her death. Even so, their love is strong enough that it extends beyond the grave and the narrator believes their two souls are still entwined. Every night, the narrator dreams of Annabel Lee and sees the brightness of her eyes in the stars. Every night, the narrator lies down by her side in her tomb by the sea.

Like many other Poe poems including "The Raven", "Ulalume", and "To One in Paradise", "Annabel Lee" follows the theme of the death of a beautiful woman,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) which Poe called "the most poetical topic in the world".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-3) Like women in many other works by Poe, she marries young and is struck with illness.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-4) The poem focuses on an ideal love which is unusually strong. In fact, the narrator's actions show that he not only loves Annabel Lee, but he worships her, something he can only do after her death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-5) The narrator admits that he and Annabel Lee were children when they fell in love, but his explanation that angels murdered her is in itself childish, suggesting he has failed to mature since then.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Empric26-6) His repetition of this assertion suggests he is trying to rationalize his own excessive feelings of loss.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Empric26-6)
Unlike "The Raven", in which the narrator believes he will "nevermore" be reunited with his love, "Annabel Lee" says the two will be together again, as not even demons "can ever dissever" their souls.

"Annabel Lee" consists of six stanzas, three with six lines, one with seven, and two with eight, with the rhyme pattern differing slightly in each one.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) Though it is not technically a ballad, Poe referred to it as one.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-7) Like a ballad, the poem uses repetition of words and phrases purposely to create its mournful effect.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) The name Annabel Lee emphasizes the letter "L", a frequent device in Poe's female characters such as "Eulalie", "Lenore", and "Ulalume".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-8)
The Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, Maryland has identified 11 versions of "Annabel Lee" that were published between 1849 and 1850.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-9) The biggest variation is in the final line:
Original manuscript: "In her tomb by the side of the sea"Alternative version: "In her tomb by the sounding sea"
Poe's wife Virginia is often assumed to be the inspiration for "Annabel Lee".

It is unclear on whom the eponymous character Annabel Lee is based.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Silverman401-10) Biographers and critics usually suggest Poe's frequent use of the "death of a beautiful woman" theme stems from the repeated loss of women throughout his own life, including his mother Eliza Poe and his foster mother Frances Allan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-11) Biographers often interpret that "Annabel Lee" was written for Poe's wife Virginia, who had died two years prior, as was suggested by poet Frances Sargent Osgood, though Osgood is herself a candidate for the poem's inspiration.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Silverman401-10) A strong case can be made for Poe's wife Virginia: She was the one he loved as a child, the only one who had been his bride, and the only one who had died.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers244-12) Autobiographical readings of the poem have also been used to support the theory that Virginia and Poe never consummated their marriage, as "Annabel Lee" was a "maiden".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-13) Critics, including T. O. Mabbott, believed that Annabel Lee was merely the product of Poe's gloomy imagination and that Annabel Lee was no real person in particular. A childhood sweetheart of Poe's named Sarah Elmira Royster believed the poem was written with her in mind[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-14) and that Poe himself said so.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-15)Sarah Helen Whitman and Sarah Anna Lewis also claimed to have inspired the poem.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Sova12-16)

Title: Annabel Lee
Chunks: 0
It was many and many a year ago,
In a kingdom by the sea,
That a maiden there lived whom you may know
By the name of Annabel Lee;
And this maiden she lived with no other thought
Than to love and be loved by me.
_I_ was a child and _she_ was a child,
In this kingdom by the sea,
But we loved with a love that was more than love—
I and my Annabel Lee—
With a love that the wingèd seraphs of Heaven
Coveted her and me.
And this was the reason that, long ago,
In this kingdom by the sea,
A wind blew out of a cloud, chilling
My beautiful Annabel Lee;
So that her highborn kinsmen came
And bore her away from me,
To shut her up in a sepulchre
In this kingdom by the sea.
The angels, not half so happy in Heaven,
Went envying her and me—
Yes!—that was the reason (as all men know,
In this kingdom by the sea)
That the wind came out of the cloud by night,
Chilling and killing my Annabel Lee.
But our love it was stronger by far than the love
Of those who were older than we—
Of many far wiser than we—
And neither the angels in Heaven above
Nor the demons down under the sea
Can ever dissever my soul from the soul
Of the beautiful Annabel Lee;
For the moon never beams, without bringing me dreams
Of the beautiful Annabel Lee;
And the stars never rise, but I feel the bright eyes
Of the beautiful Annabel Lee;
And so, all the night-tide, I lie down by the side
Of my darling—my darling—my life and my bride,
In her sepulchre there by the sea—
In her tomb by the sounding sea.

Edgar Allan Poe is known for being the Master of the Macabre, but many forget that he wrote many heartfelt and heartbreaking poems during his career. One of the best-known among these beautiful yet tragic poems is _Annabel Lee_.
The poem tells a story about a man and woman who loved each other since childhood, but are torn apart when Annabel Lee dies.
Poe was no stranger to tragedy in his personal life, and it could be that _Annabel Lee_ was written in homage to the death of his beloved wife. Over the years, the origins of _Annabel Lee_ have become something of a legend.
While there’s some gray area between fact and fiction, it is an unforgettably haunting love story. Keep reading our Valentine’s Day blog series if you’re in the mood for love stories with a spooky twist, and book a ghost tour with US Ghost Adventures to learn more haunting tales.

## Who Was Annabel Lee’s True Love?
There are many theories as to who Annabel Lee was. Some theorize that the poem was written about Poe’s wife, Virginia, who died from tuberculosis two years before Poe wrote the poem.
Others maintain that the poem was inspired by the legend of a sailor who fell in love with a woman that Poe may have heard during his time in Charleston, South Carolina.
This claim has been taken a step further, with Charleston locals alleging that the legend of Annabel Lee was based on events that happened to Poe and his lover Anna while in Charleston.
In the end, there’s no clear answer as to who Annabel Lee or her true love was. That said, there’s a belief that her spirit resides in a Charleston cemetery where she waits for her lost love.

## Edgar Allan Poe’s Last Poem
_It was many and many a year ago,_
_In a kingdom by the sea,_
_That a maiden there lived whom you may know_
_By the name of Annabel Lee;_
_And this maiden she lived with no other thought_
_Than to love and be loved by me._
So begins one of Edgar Allan Poe’s most melancholic poems. _Annabel Lee_ holds the distinction of being the last poem ever written by Poe before his untimely and mysterious death in 1849. Poe was only 40 and had been found delirious and lying in a ditch in the city of Baltimore.
The completion of _Annabel Lee_ was so recent that it was published just two days after Poe died. It’s unclear if there’s a link between his writing the poem and his unexpected demise, but Poe’s life and work both ended in a terribly sad way.
In 1849, Poe was still grieving the death of his wife, Virginia Eliza Clemm Poe. Virginia was Poe’s first cousin whom he married when she was only 13 and he was 26. They were married for 11 years until she contracted tuberculosis and died at the age of 24 in 1847.
The reference to youth and childhood in Annabel Lee has been interpreted as a reference to Virginia, whom he married when she was still a child.

## The Legend of Annabel Lee
Edgar Allan Poe joined the military in 1827 and was stationed at Fort Moultrie on Sullivan’s Island, off the coast of Charleston, South Carolina. Poe spent only a year there at the tender age of 18, but his writings make both direct and indirect references to the area. The prime example is his poem _The Gold Bug_, which is set on Sullivan’s Island.
One theory about the origins of _Annabel Lee_ is that he heard about an old legend while living on Sullivan’s Island. The legend tellsof a sailor who falls in love with a young woman but her father forbids the relationship. The woman dies brokenhearted, and the sailor goes to the cemetery to pray at her grave.
However, the father had six graves dug to confuse the sailor. One was his daughter’s, dug six feet down. The others were existing graves in the family plot where he’d had the earth turned up to make the graves look freshly dug. All unmarked, the grief-stricken sailor was unable to find his lost love.
No one knows where this horrifying tale came from, but it sounds like something that would have been inspirational to Poe.

## The Legend of Annabel Lee
### Another Version of the Tragic Love Story
Another version of this story is that Poe fell in love with a girl named Anna, the daughter of a prominent Charleston physician named Edmund Ravenel. As in the sailor’s legend, Dr. Ravenel forbids Poe from marrying the 14-year-old Anna, who was already engaged to another grown man.
Poe, in turn, was banished from Charleston, and Anna died from a fever. The dastardly Dr. Ravenel had six graves dug so that Poe could never be truly sure where Anna was buried.
In truth, there’s no evidence that Dr. Ravenel had a daughter named Anna. This legend likely evolved from a statement made by an early Poe biographer that Poe _might_ have known Dr. Ravenel. However, there’s no record of the two having ever crossed paths.

## The Ghost of Annabel Lee
Some have gone as far as to claim that Annabel Lee’s final resting place is Charleston. Charleston’s magnificent Unitarian Church has a sprawling graveyard that’s said to be home to Annabel Lee’s grave and ghost.
It’s been rumored for years that the ghost of a woman in white is seen wandering the graveyard at night. If someone attempts to make contact with her spirit, she quickly vanishes. It seems she’s only interested in seeing her true love again whom she can never find.

## A Legacy of Love With Annabel Lee
Although its origins and inspiration are murky at best, the poem’s closing lines are often seen as a clue that the story was set in Charleston and that Annabel Lee is buried in the Unitarian Church graveyard. Poe writes:
_And so, all the night-tide, I lie down by the side_
_Of my darling—my darling—my life and my bride,_
_In her sepulchre there by the sea—_
_In her tomb by the sounding sea._
The legend of Annabel Lee is a love story that only Edgar Allan Poe could tell. To learn about more tragic ghostly love stories, keep reading our Valentine’s Day blog series. Edgar Allan Poe is known for being the Master of the Macabre, but many forget that he wrote many heartfelt and heartbreaking poems during his career. One of the best-known among these beautiful yet tragic poems is _Annabel Lee_.
The poem tells a story about a man and woman who loved each other since childhood, but are torn apart when Annabel Lee dies.
Poe was no stranger to tragedy in his personal life, and it could be that _Annabel Lee_ was written in homage to the death of his beloved wife. Over the years, the origins of _Annabel Lee_ have become something of a legend.
While there’s some gray area between fact and fiction, it is an unforgettably haunting love story. Keep reading our Valentine’s Day blog series if you’re in the mood for love stories with a spooky twist, and book a ghost tour with US Ghost Adventures to learn more haunting tales.

## Who Was Annabel Lee’s True Love?
There are many theories as to who Annabel Lee was. Some theorize that the poem was written about Poe’s wife, Virginia, who died from tuberculosis two years before Poe wrote the poem.
Others maintain that the poem was inspired by the legend of a sailor who fell in love with a woman that Poe may have heard during his time in Charleston, South Carolina.
This claim has been taken a step further, with Charleston locals alleging that the legend of Annabel Lee was based on events that happened to Poe and his lover Anna while in Charleston.
In the end, there’s no clear answer as to who Annabel Lee or her true love was. That said, there’s a belief that her spirit resides in a Charleston cemetery where she waits for her lost love.

## Edgar Allan Poe’s Last Poem
_It was many and many a year ago,_
_In a kingdom by the sea,_
_That a maiden there lived whom you may know_
_By the name of Annabel Lee;_
_And this maiden she lived with no other thought_
_Than to love and be loved by me._
So begins one of Edgar Allan Poe’s most melancholic poems. _Annabel Lee_ holds the distinction of being the last poem ever written by Poe before his untimely and mysterious death in 1849. Poe was only 40 and had been found delirious and lying in a ditch in the city of Baltimore.
The completion of _Annabel Lee_ was so recent that it was published just two days after Poe died. It’s unclear if there’s a link between his writing the poem and his unexpected demise, but Poe’s life and work both ended in a terribly sad way.
In 1849, Poe was still grieving the death of his wife, Virginia Eliza Clemm Poe. Virginia was Poe’s first cousin whom he married when she was only 13 and he was 26. They were married for 11 years until she contracted tuberculosis and died at the age of 24 in 1847.
The reference to youth and childhood in Annabel Lee has been interpreted as a reference to Virginia, whom he married when she was still a child.

## The Legend of Annabel Lee
Edgar Allan Poe joined the military in 1827 and was stationed at Fort Moultrie on Sullivan’s Island, off the coast of Charleston, South Carolina. Poe spent only a year there at the tender age of 18, but his writings make both direct and indirect references to the area. The prime example is his poem _The Gold Bug_, which is set on Sullivan’s Island.
One theory about the origins of _Annabel Lee_ is that he heard about an old legend while living on Sullivan’s Island. The legend tellsof a sailor who falls in love with a young woman but her father forbids the relationship. The woman dies brokenhearted, and the sailor goes to the cemetery to pray at her grave.
However, the father had six graves dug to confuse the sailor. One was his daughter’s, dug six feet down. The others were existing graves in the family plot where he’d had the earth turned up to make the graves look freshly dug. All unmarked, the grief-stricken sailor was unable to find his lost love.
No one knows where this horrifying tale came from, but it sounds like something that would have been inspirational to Poe.

## The Legend of Annabel Lee
### Another Version of the Tragic Love Story
Another version of this story is that Poe fell in love with a girl named Anna, the daughter of a prominent Charleston physician named Edmund Ravenel. As in the sailor’s legend, Dr. Ravenel forbids Poe from marrying the 14-year-old Anna, who was already engaged to another grown man.
Poe, in turn, was banished from Charleston, and Anna died from a fever. The dastardly Dr. Ravenel had six graves dug so that Poe could never be truly sure where Anna was buried.
In truth, there’s no evidence that Dr. Ravenel had a daughter named Anna. This legend likely evolved from a statement made by an early Poe biographer that Poe _might_ have known Dr. Ravenel. However, there’s no record of the two having ever crossed paths.

## The Ghost of Annabel Lee
Some have gone as far as to claim that Annabel Lee’s final resting place is Charleston. Charleston’s magnificent Unitarian Church has a sprawling graveyard that’s said to be home to Annabel Lee’s grave and ghost.
It’s been rumored for years that the ghost of a woman in white is seen wandering the graveyard at night. If someone attempts to make contact with her spirit, she quickly vanishes. It seems she’s only interested in seeing her true love again whom she can never find.

## A Legacy of Love With Annabel Lee
Although its origins and inspiration are murky at best, the poem’s closing lines are often seen as a clue that the story was set in Charleston and that Annabel Lee is buried in the Unitarian Church graveyard. Poe writes:
_And so, all the night-tide, I lie down by the side_
_Of my darling—my darling—my life and my bride,_
_In her sepulchre there by the sea—_
_In her tomb by the sounding sea._

"**Annabel Lee**" is the last complete poem[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-1) composed by American author Edgar Allan Poe. Like many of Poe's poems, it explores the theme of the death of a beautiful woman.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) The narrator, who fell in love with Annabel Lee when they were young, has a love for her so strong that even angels are envious. He retains his love for her after her death. There has been debate over who, if anyone, was the inspiration for "Annabel Lee". Though many women have been suggested, Poe's wife Virginia Eliza Clemm Poe is one of the more credible candidates. Written in 1849, it was not published until shortly after Poe's death that same year.
Poe's manuscript for "Annabel Lee", Columbia University Rare Book and Manuscript Library
The poem's narrator describes his love for Annabel Lee, which began many years ago in a "kingdom by the sea". Though they were young, their love for each other burned with such intensity that even angels were envious. For this reason, the narrator believes the seraphim caused her death. Even so, their love is strong enough that it extends beyond the grave and the narrator believes their two souls are still entwined. Every night, the narrator dreams of Annabel Lee and sees the brightness of her eyes in the stars. Every night, the narrator lies down by her side in her tomb by the sea.
texts.1:
Like many other Poe poems including "The Raven", "Ulalume", and "To One in Paradise", "Annabel Lee" follows the theme of the death of a beautiful woman,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) which Poe called "the most poetical topic in the world".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-3) Like women in many other works by Poe, she marries young and is struck with illness.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-4) The poem focuses on an ideal love which is unusually strong. In fact, the narrator's actions show that he not only loves Annabel Lee, but he worships her, something he can only do after her death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-5) The narrator admits that he and Annabel Lee were children when they fell in love, but his explanation that angels murdered her is in itself childish, suggesting he has failed to mature since then.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Empric26-6) His repetition of this assertion suggests he is trying to rationalize his own excessive feelings of loss.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Empric26-6)
Unlike "The Raven", in which the narrator believes he will "nevermore" be reunited with his love, "Annabel Lee" says the two will be together again, as not even demons "can ever dissever" their souls.
texts.2:
"Annabel Lee" consists of six stanzas, three with six lines, one with seven, and two with eight, with the rhyme pattern differing slightly in each one.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) Though it is not technically a ballad, Poe referred to it as one.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-7) Like a ballad, the poem uses repetition of words and phrases purposely to create its mournful effect.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) The name Annabel Lee emphasizes the letter "L", a frequent device in Poe's female characters such as "Eulalie", "Lenore", and "Ulalume".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-8)
The Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, Maryland has identified 11 versions of "Annabel Lee" that were published between 1849 and 1850.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-9) The biggest variation is in the final line:
Original manuscript: "In her tomb by the side of the sea"Alternative version: "In her tomb by the sounding sea"
Poe's wife Virginia is often assumed to be the inspiration for "Annabel Lee".
texts.3: It is unclear on whom the eponymous character Annabel Lee is based.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Silverman401-10) Biographers and critics usually suggest Poe's frequent use of the "death of a beautiful woman" theme stems from the repeated loss of women throughout his own life, including his mother Eliza Poe and his foster mother Frances Allan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-11) Biographers often interpret that "Annabel Lee" was written for Poe's wife Virginia, who had died two years prior, as was suggested by poet Frances Sargent Osgood, though Osgood is herself a candidate for the poem's inspiration.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Silverman401-10) A strong case can be made for Poe's wife Virginia: She was the one he loved as a child, the only one who had been his bride, and the only one who had died.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers244-12) Autobiographical readings of the poem have also been used to support the theory that Virginia and Poe never consummated their marriage, as "Annabel Lee" was a "maiden".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-13) Critics, including T. O. Mabbott, believed that Annabel Lee was merely the product of Poe's gloomy imagination and that Annabel Lee was no real person in particular. A childhood sweetheart of Poe's named Sarah Elmira Royster believed the poem was written with her in mind[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-14) and that Poe himself said so.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-15)Sarah Helen Whitman and Sarah Anna Lewis also claimed to have inspired the poem.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Sova12-16)

There are many theories as to who Annabel Lee was. Some theorize that the poem was written about Poe’s wife, Virginia, who died from tuberculosis two years before Poe wrote the poem.
Others maintain that the poem was inspired by the legend of a sailor who fell in love with a woman that Poe may have heard during his time in Charleston, South Carolina.
This claim has been taken a step further, with Charleston locals alleging that the legend of Annabel Lee was based on events that happened to Poe and his lover Anna while in Charleston.
In the end, there’s no clear answer as to who Annabel Lee or her true love was. That said, there’s a belief that her spirit resides in a Charleston cemetery where she waits for her lost love.

## Edgar Allan Poe’s Last Poem
_It was many and many a year ago,_
_In a kingdom by the sea,_
_That a maiden there lived whom you may know_
_By the name of Annabel Lee;_
_And this maiden she lived with no other thought_
_Than to love and be loved by me._
So begins one of Edgar Allan Poe’s most melancholic poems. _Annabel Lee_ holds the distinction of being the last poem ever written by Poe before his untimely and mysterious death in 1849. Poe was only 40 and had been found delirious and lying in a ditch in the city of Baltimore.
The completion of _Annabel Lee_ was so recent that it was published just two days after Poe died. It’s unclear if there’s a link between his writing the poem and his unexpected demise, but Poe’s life and work both ended in a terribly sad way.
In 1849, Poe was still grieving the death of his wife, Virginia Eliza Clemm Poe. Virginia was Poe’s first cousin whom he married when she was only 13 and he was 26. They were married for 11 years until she contracted tuberculosis and died at the age of 24 in 1847.
The reference to youth and childhood in Annabel Lee has been interpreted as a reference to Virginia, whom he married when she was still a child.

## The Legend of Annabel Lee
Edgar Allan Poe joined the military in 1827 and was stationed at Fort Moultrie on Sullivan’s Island, off the coast of Charleston, South Carolina. Poe spent only a year there at the tender age of 18, but his writings make both direct and indirect references to the area. The prime example is his poem _The Gold Bug_, which is set on Sullivan’s Island.
One theory about the origins of _Annabel Lee_ is that he heard about an old legend while living on Sullivan’s Island. The legend tellsof a sailor who falls in love with a young woman but her father forbids the relationship. The woman dies brokenhearted, and the sailor goes to the cemetery to pray at her grave.
However, the father had six graves dug to confuse the sailor. One was his daughter’s, dug six feet down. The others were existing graves in the family plot where he’d had the earth turned up to make the graves look freshly dug. All unmarked, the grief-stricken sailor was unable to find his lost love.
No one knows where this horrifying tale came from, but it sounds like something that would have been inspirational to Poe.

### Another Version of the Tragic Love Story
Another version of this story is that Poe fell in love with a girl named Anna, the daughter of a prominent Charleston physician named Edmund Ravenel. As in the sailor’s legend, Dr. Ravenel forbids Poe from marrying the 14-year-old Anna, who was already engaged to another grown man.
Poe, in turn, was banished from Charleston, and Anna died from a fever. The dastardly Dr. Ravenel had six graves dug so that Poe could never be truly sure where Anna was buried.
In truth, there’s no evidence that Dr. Ravenel had a daughter named Anna. This legend likely evolved from a statement made by an early Poe biographer that Poe _might_ have known Dr. Ravenel. However, there’s no record of the two having ever crossed paths.

## The Ghost of Annabel Lee
Some have gone as far as to claim that Annabel Lee’s final resting place is Charleston. Charleston’s magnificent Unitarian Church has a sprawling graveyard that’s said to be home to Annabel Lee’s grave and ghost.
It’s been rumored for years that the ghost of a woman in white is seen wandering the graveyard at night. If someone attempts to make contact with her spirit, she quickly vanishes. It seems she’s only interested in seeing her true love again whom she can never find.

"**Annabel Lee**" is the last complete poem[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-1) composed by American author Edgar Allan Poe. Like many of Poe's poems, it explores the theme of the death of a beautiful woman.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) The narrator, who fell in love with Annabel Lee when they were young, has a love for her so strong that even angels are envious. He retains his love for her after her death. There has been debate over who, if anyone, was the inspiration for "Annabel Lee". Though many women have been suggested, Poe's wife Virginia Eliza Clemm Poe is one of the more credible candidates. Written in 1849, it was not published until shortly after Poe's death that same year.
Poe's manuscript for "Annabel Lee", Columbia University Rare Book and Manuscript Library
The poem's narrator describes his love for Annabel Lee, which began many years ago in a "kingdom by the sea". Though they were young, their love for each other burned with such intensity that even angels were envious. For this reason, the narrator believes the seraphim caused her death. Even so, their love is strong enough that it extends beyond the grave and the narrator believes their two souls are still entwined. Every night, the narrator dreams of Annabel Lee and sees the brightness of her eyes in the stars. Every night, the narrator lies down by her side in her tomb by the sea.

Like many other Poe poems including "The Raven", "Ulalume", and "To One in Paradise", "Annabel Lee" follows the theme of the death of a beautiful woman,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) which Poe called "the most poetical topic in the world".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-3) Like women in many other works by Poe, she marries young and is struck with illness.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-4) The poem focuses on an ideal love which is unusually strong. In fact, the narrator's actions show that he not only loves Annabel Lee, but he worships her, something he can only do after her death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-5) The narrator admits that he and Annabel Lee were children when they fell in love, but his explanation that angels murdered her is in itself childish, suggesting he has failed to mature since then.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Empric26-6) His repetition of this assertion suggests he is trying to rationalize his own excessive feelings of loss.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Empric26-6)
Unlike "The Raven", in which the narrator believes he will "nevermore" be reunited with his love, "Annabel Lee" says the two will be together again, as not even demons "can ever dissever" their souls.

"Annabel Lee" consists of six stanzas, three with six lines, one with seven, and two with eight, with the rhyme pattern differing slightly in each one.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) Though it is not technically a ballad, Poe referred to it as one.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-7) Like a ballad, the poem uses repetition of words and phrases purposely to create its mournful effect.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers243-2) The name Annabel Lee emphasizes the letter "L", a frequent device in Poe's female characters such as "Eulalie", "Lenore", and "Ulalume".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-8)
The Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, Maryland has identified 11 versions of "Annabel Lee" that were published between 1849 and 1850.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-9) The biggest variation is in the final line:
Original manuscript: "In her tomb by the side of the sea"Alternative version: "In her tomb by the sounding sea"
Poe's wife Virginia is often assumed to be the inspiration for "Annabel Lee".

It is unclear on whom the eponymous character Annabel Lee is based.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Silverman401-10) Biographers and critics usually suggest Poe's frequent use of the "death of a beautiful woman" theme stems from the repeated loss of women throughout his own life, including his mother Eliza Poe and his foster mother Frances Allan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-11) Biographers often interpret that "Annabel Lee" was written for Poe's wife Virginia, who had died two years prior, as was suggested by poet Frances Sargent Osgood, though Osgood is herself a candidate for the poem's inspiration.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Silverman401-10) A strong case can be made for Poe's wife Virginia: She was the one he loved as a child, the only one who had been his bride, and the only one who had died.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Meyers244-12) Autobiographical readings of the poem have also been used to support the theory that Virginia and Poe never consummated their marriage, as "Annabel Lee" was a "maiden".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-13) Critics, including T. O. Mabbott, believed that Annabel Lee was merely the product of Poe's gloomy imagination and that Annabel Lee was no real person in particular. A childhood sweetheart of Poe's named Sarah Elmira Royster believed the poem was written with her in mind[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-14) and that Poe himself said so.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-15)Sarah Helen Whitman and Sarah Anna Lewis also claimed to have inspired the poem.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabel_Lee#cite_note-Sova12-16)
